hints.title: Expose the three choices in order
hints.body: The original has the order: for every positive N, there exists a positive K, such that for every positive m the expression is not prime.
hints.recap: Writing the quantifiers first makes their nesting visible.
hints.pitfall: K can depend on N; the order of choices must not be swapped.
hints.pause: Write the three quantifiers in the same order before negating.

recall.reminder: Read both quantifier order and allowed domains.

hints.title: Push the negation through in order
hints.body: Start with the outermost choice, applying not-every becomes some-not and not-some becomes every-not, then repeat at the next nested choice.
hints.recap: Negation changes quantifiers without changing their order.
hints.pitfall: The later choices may depend on earlier ones.
hints.pause: Write the new quantifier chain while keeping the final property temporarily unchanged.

recall.reminder: Negation changes quantifiers without changing their order.

hints.title: Finish at the predicate
hints.body: Once the negation reaches the final property, negate that property and retain the positive-integer domains of all variables.
hints.recap: Both the quantifiers and the final predicate must be handled.
hints.pitfall: Not-prime is not the same as composite because one is also non-prime.
hints.pause: Assemble the complete negated sentence and compare every scope with the options.

recall.reminder: Both the quantifiers and the final predicate must be handled.

solution:
The negation is: there exists a positive integer N such that for every positive integer K, there exists a positive integer m for which N(Km+1)−1 is prime.

The chain every–some–every becomes some–every–some, and not prime becomes prime. No primality computation is required. Answer F.
knowledgePattern: Negate three nested quantifiers and the primality predicate
